text.p: Spring! Time to trash those rusty garden chairs and get plastic lawn furniture.
But be careful: you may be about to throw out an antique. Scrape off the rust and you might find the name of an 18th century iron foundry, which means your rusty trash could be treasure.

"They can be quite valuable because if they're antique, a lot of pieces didn't make it over time outdoors. So what's left is pretty scarce and getting scarcer," said Elizabeth Schumacher, a dealer in Gulph Mills, Pa. (610-825-5525).

A late 19th century 40-inch cast iron bench stamped James W. Carr, Richmond, Va. is worth about $4,000, according to "The Official Price Guide to Garden Furniture and Accessories" by Margaret Lindquist (919-933-3179) and Judith Wells, published by House of Collectibles in New York.

Expect your rusty iron bench -- if it's in good condition and cleaned up -- to be worth about $1,000 or more if it's marked J.W. Fiske of New York, Wood & Perot of Philadelphia, Coalbrookdale of England or Val d'Osne of France.
Prices of antique, or just old, benches and other garden accessories have risen steadily as Americans have rediscovered the pleasures of the outdoors and made creating their own Eden a priority.
"If you're going to have a pretty garden and flowers, you need one thing to make your garden different, that defines your garden," said Elaine Whitmire, a specialist at Sotheby's.
That may be an iron or wooden bench, statue, birdbath or lion's head -- old or new.
But as the gardening bug bites -- the hobby is addictive, just ask any gardener -- reclaimers of Eden awake to the idea that Paradise was not only planted and pretty but also pre-plastic.

"If I put in an old bench with lichen, it speaks age. It looks like the garden has been there much longer. It gives an established look," said Barbara Israel, a dealer in Catona, N.Y. (914-232-42710).

More and more aspiring Adams and Eves want to add instant history to their suburban plots, driving up prices of old marble, zinc, limestone and cast iron statues, furniture, fountains, urns, gates, aviaries, lanterns and even tools.
Sotheby's New York has seen sales at its annual garden statuary auctions rise steadily since 1990, and is holding the event for the first time in the affluent enclave of Greenwich, Conn., on June 15.

A pair of bronze lions by A. Durenne, Sommevoire is expected to fetch up to $30,000; a 1946 "Pegasus" marble statue by American sculptor William Wheeler, $6,000; four marble female figures representing the Four Seasons, circa 1900, $20,000; and a 19th century marble lion mask, $6,000.

For smaller budgets, Marston Luce, a dealer in Washington, sells antique watering cans for $185 to $6,000. Those signed by the maker are worth more. An antique child's wooden wheelbarrow, with the original paint, cost $500. Ten years ago, it would have sold for only $100 to $150, Luce said.
Even hand-made metal tools with a patina are in demand for use as wall-hangings reminiscent of another age.
"The value is more aesthetic. Old copper, a beautiful green colour, has a quality that's very romantic," Luce said.
Presumably, you won't find more than rusty mass-produced tools and machines in your shed, or damaged painted cement elves and mushrooms in your garden.
Iron or lead chairs and benches are more common and, even if mere reproductions, are so popular that they have dampened the value of their antique counterparts, Whitmire said.
Collectors can scour for undervalued treasures at country fairs and auctions, especially in lower-priced regions where gardening hasn't become a craze.
Make sure what is described as a marble figure is really marble. "Marble is the most expensive, bronze is second and cast iron the least," said Whitmire.

For investment-minded gardeners, a white marble figure of a female that could have sold for $10,000 a decade ago is now worth $20,000, Whitmire said. But that's because of a spurt of interest from Japanese buyers, she said.
Cast stone is worth far less than a carved stone figure.
Among benches, a marble one costs about $6,000, an unusual cast iron one $3,000, and a reproduction $700, said Whitmire.
Several books are available, including "Antique Garden Ornament" by John Davis and "Antiques from the Garden" by Alistair Morris, both from the Antique Collectors Club.
